Where are they now : Mpho and Mphonyana

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Its a story that captured the attention of many in the late 80ds, siamese twins joined at the head- Mphoand Mphonyana...We revisit a story that inspired a nation living through dark times.

Unique Selling Point:
it is the late 80s and South Africa is a country in turmoil,the apartheid government is fighting in the Angolan who and almost
daily - limpet mine bombs are going off in the country...There is great tension for everyone...

But for a while the country's gaze shifts... word of a set of conjoined/ siamese twins being born in Klerksdorp gets everyone buzzing,but it the soon to be -groundbreaking surgery to separate the twins that captures the imagination of the populace, as well as the medical community. The operation would be difficult as the twins share a vital artery, as well as some brain matter.

A 40 men team made up of the best surgeon in the country was assembled headed by the famed professor of neurosurgery, Robert Lipschitz, and the equally-famed Professor Sam Mokgokong.

For 16 months, the twins shared the sagital sinus, a major vein that drains blood from the brain, as well as a section of skull and a large amount of brain tissue.

It was touch and go. Professor Lipschitz had previously given the twins a less than 50-50 chance of surviving the operation.

The world followed the proceedings with bated breath as the team entered the theatre. Seven-and-half hours later, they emerged triumphant, to the applause of a waiting nation.

There was dancing in the streets. Baragwanath Hospital could now stand shoulder to shoulder with other major hospitals. The self-esteem of everyone involved went through the roof.

To date the picture of Mpho and Mphonyana has for the past two decades become something of a pop iconograph, adorning millions of working-class township and rural homes...It reminds us of a period where once, just once we were pulling in the same direction and had a sense of "Seeing each other" not as them...The Mathibela twins were just babies even though they were black...We were rooting for them to pull through.

Despite Mphonyana dying of pneumonia just a year after the separation, Mpho would go on to live a fulfilling life,passing on after an epileptic seizure...she diesin 2021...she lived up to 34 years of age.


Summary:
We will be speaking to the Mathibela family,where we will be speaking to Dr Percy Miller who is one of the last members of the team that separated the twins...We will be facilitating a reunion between the Mathibela Family, as well as Dr Percy Miller at Bara Hospital.

Script :Mpho and Mphonyana


VO It's 1986 and South Africa is in a State of emergency…there is violence and bloodshed on the streets , it will be another 4 years before the unbanning of liberation movements and the release of Nelson Mandela.

[breather]

VO But in Klerksdorp, in the North West, the birth of a set of twins has everyone buzzing.

V/O …the newborns are conjoined at the head and were a rare sight for many South Africans


Link : Their story dominated the news cycle in South Africa for months, they captured our hearts and captivated an entire nation—the story of iconic twins Mpho and Mphonyana Mathibela.
[breather]

V/O With daily updates in Newspapers ,Television and radio stations their story was a welcomed distraction from the violence and chaos in the country.
VO: Almost two years after their historic birth, a team of highly trained medical specialists gathered at the then-Baragwanath Hospital in Gauteng for a groundbreaking surgery… to separate Mpho and Mphonyana for the first time in their lives.
Upsound Claire and Sophie looking through pictures:34:31 This is in the morning 5 am, on the way to the operation , we were praying before they got inside the theatre.

[transition here]
VO: The operation was a first of its kind in South Africa and 34 years since the twins were separated … We wanted to catch up with the Mathibela family and the medical team that made history.
V/O After weeks of research our search led us to Klerksdorp where Mpho and Mphonyana were born on the 9th of December 1986, and where their mother Sophie Mathibela still lives.
Upsound Claire: what was your first reaction when you saw them?
Upsound Sophie : I was scared but I told myself that even if I was scared there is no way around it, they are my children, There is nothing I can do, or run away-they are my children.

VO Sharing a sagittal sinus- a major vein that drains blood from the brain, a section of the skull, and a large amount of brain tissue, specialists didn't give the twins long to live

Upsound Sophie 04:38 :I would pray and I would run out of prayer, sometimes I would wake up in the morning, the sun would rise and set without me sleeping. It was difficult.

VO: Her prayers were finally answered when a team of forty of the best surgeons and nurses in the country, assembled in Soweto to attempt this innovative, but risky surgery.

Upsound Sophie :I believed in the doctors and agreed to go ahead with the operation.



Upsound Claire: How big was the team and who were the people that made up teams- in terms of expertise?

Upsound Dr Percy Miller : I was a young registrar at the time,it was a massive team .It had the neurosurgeons ,four consultants and the boss, Professor Lipschitz. It had plastic surgeons b the most important was the anesthetist there were three or four anesthetists because once the kids had been separated, the two cribs had to be rolled apart and each kid had to be worked on at the same time.

VO Dr. Percy Miller is one of the last remaining members of that team.
Upsound Dr Percy Miller : The main draining vein from the brain is common to both twins. So one draining vein runs between both heads. Now, if their brain gets damaged or disturbed, then their brain swells because there's no way for the blood to go and that child is going to be very badly damaged or die.
Upsound Dr Percy Miller: So you have to work out a way to split the vein in two so that each kid gets a bit of vein drainage, to do that is really complex technically.
VO A complex operation that had many South Africans on the edge of their seats.

Upsound Claire : Doctor, the whole country was waiting with bated breath. There was so much media attention. Did that add any pressure to the team
Upsound Dr Percy miller : There was there was a lot of pressure because,it made everything much more tense. There were so many reporters outside, and by the time we came out, about 5 / 6, it had doubled.
V/O As a young SABC news TV reporter, Karien van der Merwe broke the story to a deeply divided nation.
Upsound Karien Van der Merwe : It became international news. And then I realized and people started recognizing me on the street because I was in their homes every day telling the story.
Upsound Karien van der Merwe : This was 1988 and we were so far away from the new South Africa, but Mpho and Mphonyana united South Africans because for once people black and white cared about the same two little children. And it was just amazing.

V/O After ten grueling hours Mpho and Mphonyana were separated.
Upsound Dr Percy Miller :They were all on ventilators and tubes and things, but they looked good. So by the next morning, we could say, okay, it actually looks like it's winning.
V/O While the operation had been successful, complications are always a risk ,and tragically a year after the procedure Mphonyana died of pneumonia.
Upsound Sophie: The weak one was Mphonyana. Mpho was alright, she was able to walk ,Mpho could sit at a table and eat, she could take herself to the toilet, she could bathE herself but she was slow.
V/O Mpho went on to live to the age of 35, while still tragically short, it was still a relatively full life for someone who had once faced seemingly insurmountable odds.
Upsound Sophie 26:01 Mpho was sick for a short time , , she would tell me her legs are painful ,she told me that her legs aren’t moving , on Saturday it got worse she couldn’t get off the bed.
Upsound Sophie Mpho died on the 6th of August on a Friday.
VO Her death was especially devastating for her older sister Kedisaletse Mathibela-Mokgobi
UpsoundKedisaletse Mathibela-Mokgobi : 05:30 She had love she liked praying and at night she would pray for me.
Upsound Claire : Did it break your heart?
Upsound Kedisaletse Mathibela-Mokgobi 09:27 A lot 10:14 Mpho and I were close a lot.
VO Still coming to terms with Mpho’s death , the Mathibela family say they are grateful to the medical team that changed their lives. Carte Blanche invited both Sophie and Dr Miller back to Bara for a reunion that is 35 years in the making.

Upsound Claire :00:19:32:00 - 00:19:40:16: We thought we should just remind South Africa about the importance of this story and the incredible medical professionals that did it. But we went a step further,Mpho amd Mphonyana’s mother is here!
Upsound Sophie : It is a long story
Upsound- Reunion : Claire Its a long story
Upsound - Reunion : Dr Miller It was in ward 7
Upsound- Reunion Sophie :Laughs] Yes it was in ward 7
Upsound - Reunion Dr Miller: And there was a little roommateat the side, I remember her feeding the kids everyday.So there you go

Upsoud-Reunion Claire: A life you changed
Upsound Reunion Dr Miller: History

V/O History that began with two special girls, a medical team capable of miracles, and a country yearning for hope.
